html:
Saint-Domingue was the French colony on the western third of the island of Hispaniola, from the 1600s to 1804. It grew into the richest colony in the world, and then, through the only slave revolt in history to found a state, became Haiti.

French buccaneers settled the empty western coast in the mid-1600s, after Spain had cleared it to stop smuggling; see Spanish Hispaniola. In the Peace of Ryswick of 1697 Spain accepted French rule there, while the east stayed the Spanish colony of Santo Domingo.

In the 1700s planters covered the plains with sugar and the hills with coffee. By the 1780s Saint-Domingue produced a large share of the world's sugar and coffee, more than all the British islands together. Its wealth rested on about half a million enslaved Africans, worked so hard that many died within a few years and had to be replaced by new shiploads through the Atlantic slave trade. Society was split between white planters, a large group of free people of colour, and the enslaved majority.

In August 1791 the enslaved rose in the north; see Haitian Revolution. France abolished slavery in 1794, and the former slave Toussaint Louverture took control of the colony. Napoleon sent an army in 1802 to restore French rule, but it was beaten, and on 1 January 1804 Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared the independence of Haiti.
sum: Saint-Domingue was the French colony on the western third of the island of Hispaniola, from the 1600s to 1804. It grew into the richest colony in the world, and then, through the only slave revolt in history to found a state, became Haiti.
